You are very incorrect in assuming that there are two sides to vaccine science. Vaccines are built upon the workings of the immune system and "tricking" the immune system to believe the body has been infected by an infectious organism when it really hasn't. In order to understand vaccines, you must have a correct understanding of the immune system.

I often find that anti-vaxxers have no idea what they're talking about, or they know just enough to both be incredibly incorrect and sway others who know less than they do. That's the problem with a lot of the individuals in the anti-vax movement, fundamentally, they have no understanding of the science involved. They read ingredients and see terms like "formaldehyde" (a bi-product of many cellular processes in your own body, by the way) and freak out because formaldehyde is also a poison. I have no doubt that they do their own research, but fundamentally the information they are using in their research is incredibly flawed and incorrect, for example, they'll link stories from pop-science sites such as www.naturalnews.com or www.mercola.com.

Below is a little blurb I wrote about how the immune system works in terms of vaccines. It's over simplified, but for they lay, it's a pretty good overview of the immune system:

Leukocytes are white blood cells. The five types of leukocytes are: neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils. Neutrophils are generally involved in the innate immune response (meaning they just kind of circulate and their lysozymes kill bacteria). Monocytes move to different tissues and become macrophages (basically big giant eaters of pathogens). Basophils are generally involved in the inflammatory response. Eosinophils are generally involved in allergic reactions and fight against parasites especially worms. This is a gross over-simplification of SOME of the cells in the immune systemt.

Lymphocytes are involved in both humoral and cell-mediated immunity, it depends on which type of lymphocyte you’re talking about. B-type lymphocytes are involved in humoral immunity because they are the cells that produce antibodies. T-type lymphocytes are involved in cell-mediated immunity because the CD8+ cytotoxic T cells destroy pathogens. CD4+ helper cells are also part of the cell-mediated immune response and they "help" B and CD8+ cells recognize which antigen they want produce antibodies against or look for in order to destroy.

In other words, vaccines work because of BOTH humoral AND cell-mediated immunity, because both B lymphocytes and T lymphocytes are involved. B cells also produce immunological memory. That is, the body keeps a store of these cells available in case you come into contact with the pathogen again. CD4+ cells are also involved because they activate the memory B cells to reproduce and produce the necessary antibodies they already know how to make. Humoral and cell-mediated immunity do not work separately, they work in conjunction with each other.

B type lymphocytes produce antibodies that are specific to an antigen (usually a protein, or other marker from the cell surface of the infectious agent). Once you come into contact with the same pathogen, the B cells are activated (with or without the help of CD4+ helper T lymphocytes). Next these cells proliferate and make copies of themselves. Next, the cells differentiate into plasma cells and memory cells. The plasma cells produce a huge number of antibodies but eventually die. The memory B cells live for years and lie dormant until activated by the same antigen to produce antibodies.

Cell-mediated immunity is also involved in the immunity elicited by vaccinations. Vaccines take advantage of cell-mediated immunity because the CD4+ T helper lymphocytes are able to activate the B cells that you already have in your body that are capable of producing the antibodies needed to fight off the infectious agent. Again, cell-mediated immunity is the realm of the T-lymphocytes ( CD4+ helper T-cells).

Humoral immunity is actually more efficient because when exposed to the infectious agent the second time around, the body produces many many many times more antibodies than the first time around and the response is much faster. The antibodies produced by this reaction are sufficient to keep an infection at bay and to induce herd immunity because you have many more antibodies floating around in your body than you do individual cells. Again, you are falsely discounting or trying to make it seem like humoral immunity is not sufficient enough to produce herd immunity, but it is. Antibodies work by neutralizing a threat (for example, they can block a receptor on the virus or bacteria), agglutination (they can get the infectious cells to stick together), precipitation, and activation of complement.

Vaccines work because they take advantage of immunological memory. Your body reacts the same way to a vaccine as it does to an infectious agent minus the infection. Some vaccines contain the entire organism and other contain antigens specific to all forms of that infectious agent. Think about it this way: if you ever had chicken pox and came into contact with someone else who had chicken pox, you wouldn't get the chicken pox infection again because your body has the antibodies to chicken pox already produced. Vaccines work the same way, you have those antibody-producing B cells stored in a pool in your body, therefore your body knows exactly how to handle that infectious agent when you come into contact with it.

My point is, find a real source. I'm sure there are much more reputable sources on the subject than this garbage. Penn and Teller have no place in a sub called "critical thinking".
